newsitem.title: USA: U.S. official optimistic about trade despite dlr.
newsitem.headline: U.S. official optimistic about trade despite dlr.

text.p: A Senior U.S. official on Wednesday brushed aside concerns that the resurgent dollar will hurt U.S. trade and said he expects a steady improvement in American sales abroad that will help reduce the deficit.

A pick up in economic growth in Europe, Mexico and Canada, coupled with expected structural economic changes in Japan, bode well for U.S. exports and will more than offset any expected drag from the strengthening dollar, he told Reuters.

"I don't think that what we've seen in the exchange rate, or what we might in any scenario expect to see, is a more compelling influence on trade than those other factors," the official, who asked not to be identified, said.
"The other forces are much more powerful and much more enduring," he added.

Fears that the stronger dollar could undermine U.S. competitiveness were fanned by news last week of a much higher than expected August trade deficit of $10.83 billion. U.S. auto manufacturers have complained loudly that the strong dollar -- which jumped to a 33-month high against the yen on Wednesday -- would hurt their hard won-sales to Japan.
Republican Presidential candidate Bob Dole added fuel to the fire by declaring that the trade deficit this year will hit an all-time high.
But the senior administration official said he was optimistic about Japan because of structural changes that will open its markets up to more U.S. goods.
"Japan is one of the great growth markets for U.S. exports because they are going to have to adapt or die," the U.S. official said.
"Changes made to date in opening the japanese market have already produced sizeable improvements (in U.S. exports)," he noted.
Prospects for greater economic growth in Europe and North America also improve the trade outlook, he said.
"I don't necessarily think that they are going to fire the rockets and take off like a new Asian rim, but they are at the low points in their (business) cycle," he said.
"I think we are only beginning to enter a period where all three of the North American Free Trade Agreement economies (Canada, U.S. and Mexico) are growing together," he said.
Those factors coupled with improvements in U.S. business productivity all point to a better trade picture, he said.
